Read the three headline specs before the rankings

Every scope below is sold on bandwidth, sample rate and channel count, and beginners are often oversold on the first while overlooking how the second falls when more channels are switched on. If those terms are new, start with what oscilloscope bandwidth means and what GSa/s means, then the oscilloscope buying guide for memory depth, triggering and probes. Not sure you need a scope at all? Our oscilloscope vs multimeter comparison shows what each tool can and can't see.

Our three hands-on tested picks each have a deeper write-up: the Rigol DS1054Z review, the Siglent SDS1104X-E review and Rigol DHO804 vs DS1054Z, which weighs 12-bit resolution against the older classic. If your first projects are microcontrollers, the best oscilloscope for Arduino projects ranks for that work, and the home electronics lab guide looks at a scope as part of a full bench. When it arrives, how to use an oscilloscope takes you from probe compensation to your first stable trigger.

Bandwidth across the range

The picks span more than three orders of magnitude, from pocket testers rated in kilohertz to benchtops rated in hundreds of megahertz. The kilohertz-class tools are fine for audio, sensors and learning what a waveform looks like, but they can't show a microcontroller's clock edges. Anything from about 50 MHz up handles the typical hobby bench.

What happens to sample rate with four channels on

The headline sample rate usually applies to one channel. Most scopes share their converters, so the rate per channel drops as you switch channels on. With all four in use, the Siglent SDS1104X-E keeps 500 MSa/s per channel, twice the DS1054Z's 250 MSa/s. As a rough check, a scope wants several samples per cycle of the fastest signal: 250 MSa/s on a 25 MHz signal gives 10 samples per cycle, enough to see its shape.

#5Best 12-bit Upgrade4.8★★★★★Hands-on Tested

Rigol DHO804

Four channels, 12-bit resolution and a 7-inch touchscreen in a compact body that runs from USB-C power.

Best for:Hobbyists who want 12-bit detail and a touchscreen

The DHO804 brings 12-bit vertical resolution to a beginner budget: 70 MHz, four channels, up to 1.25 GSa/s and 25 Mpts with one channel on, a 7-inch 1024 × 600 capacitive touchscreen, HDMI output and serial decoding of UART, I2C, SPI, CAN and parallel buses. It is powered over USB-C, so it can run from a portable power source. There is no built-in signal generator or logic channels, and sample rate and memory fall as you enable more channels (312.5 MSa/s and 5 Mpts with all four on).

Rigol DS1102Z-E

Rigol's two-channel, 100 MHz benchtop with deep memory, for people who never need a third or fourth channel.

The DS1102Z-E is a two-channel version of the DS1000Z platform with 100 MHz bandwidth: 1 GSa/s on one channel (500 MSa/s on two), 24 Mpts of memory per Rigol's datasheet, a 7-inch 800 × 480 display, up to 30,000 waveforms per second and standard decoding of UART, I2C, SPI and parallel buses. Siglent SDS1102CML+

A simple 100 MHz, two-channel benchtop with a frequency counter and pass/fail testing, but shallow memory.

Methodology

How we chose

We compared bandwidth, channel count, and sample rate against the signals beginners and hobbyists actually measure, from audio-range work to microcontroller debugging.

Specs from the sourceEvery spec is checked against the manufacturer's official product page or datasheet and the official Amazon listing. Where sources disagree, we say so.
Fit over feature countEach pick earns its place for a specific kind of buyer, and we name who should skip it, rather than ranking on spec-sheet length.
Owner feedback, cross-checkedWe look for patterns in verified-purchase reviews to catch reliability issues that spec sheets never show.
No sponsored picksWe earn mainly from Amazon affiliate commissions and may also show display ads from Google. No brand or advertiser can pay for a spot, a ranking or a badge, and ads never affect our picks.

Picks marked "Hands-on Tested" have been bought and tested by us; the rest are desk research. A pick only carries that badge once we have actually bought and tested that unit. More on how we research.

Questions

Frequently asked questions

How much bandwidth do I actually need?+

For general electronics, Arduino/microcontroller work, and audio circuits, 50-100MHz is plenty. You only need higher bandwidth (200MHz+) for RF work or very high-speed digital signals. A common rule of thumb is a bandwidth about five times the highest frequency you need to see clearly, so square edges keep their shape instead of rounding off.

Does channel count matter for a beginner?+

Yes, more than people expect. Even basic debugging often benefits from comparing two signals at once (e.g., clock vs. data line), so we'd recommend at least 2 channels, with 4 giving real long-term flexibility. Four channels let you watch an SPI bus's clock, data and chip-select lines together, or a power supply's input, output and switching node in one capture.

What is the difference between an 8-bit and a 12-bit oscilloscope?+

Bit depth sets how finely the scope slices the vertical scale. An 8-bit converter has 256 levels and a 12-bit one has 4,096. Across an 8 V full screen, that is about 31 mV per step versus about 2 mV, so 12-bit scopes like the Rigol DHO800 series show small ripple and noise that an 8-bit scope blurs into a thick trace. For logic and timing work, 8-bit is fine.

How much memory depth does a beginner oscilloscope need?+

Memory decides how long the scope can capture at full speed: capture time equals memory divided by sample rate. At 1 GSa/s, 24 Mpts holds 24 ms, while a 10K-point record holds just 10 µs before the scope must slow its sampling. Deep memory matters for serial packets, power-up sequences and intermittent glitches. For looking at repeating waveforms, a shallow record is less of a handicap.

Can I measure mains voltage with a beginner oscilloscope?+

Not directly with standard probes. On a mains-powered bench scope, every probe's ground clip is tied to earth, so clipping it onto a live or neutral conductor can create a short circuit, destroy the probe and injure you. Use a properly rated differential probe or an isolated instrument, and treat a 100X probe as extra voltage range, not isolation. If you are unsure, have a qualified electrician take the measurement.

Is a handheld or USB oscilloscope good enough to learn on?+

For learning the basics, yes, with limits. Handhelds like the FNIRSI 2C53T or OWON HDS272S are portable and add a multimeter, but their small screens and short records make detail hard to see. USB scopes such as the PicoScope 2204A use your laptop's screen and polished software but need a computer. If you will mostly work at a bench, a 7-inch benchtop is easier to learn on.
